Most companies don't stall between $50M and $500M because of strategy. They stall because leadership didn't scale with the business.

Here's what that actually looks like in practice: the decisions that got you to $50M were made by a small group of people who knew everything. At $200M, that same approach creates bottlenecks, burnout, and blind spots.

Strive Health recently expanded its executive team specifically to support its next phase of growth. That move isn't administrative. It's a leadership architecture decision.

Three things scaling leaders get wrong:

1. They promote operators into leadership roles without changing what those roles demand.
2. They treat culture as a values poster instead of a daily operating decision.
3. They wait until the pain is obvious before restructuring how decisions get made.

The leaders who successfully navigate this range don't just manage growth. They redesign themselves and their teams to meet it.

What's the biggest leadership shift your company had to make when revenue doubled?

#Leadership #Scaling #ExecutiveLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes a point that every scaling company needs to hear: executives who deploy AI without first understanding how it changes decision-making at the top will create more chaos than competitive advantage.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Companies between $50M and $500M are under enormous pressure to adopt new tools fast. But when leadership hasn't defined who owns decisions, what accountability looks like, and how information flows, adding AI accelerates the dysfunction.

Technology doesn't fix a leadership gap. It exposes one.

Before your next AI initiative, ask whether your leadership structure is ready to absorb it. If the answer is uncertain, that's where the work starts.

Most business owners think their exit multiple is determined at the closing table. It is not. It is determined two to three years before the deal even starts.

J.P. Morgan's private bank recently outlined how exit strategy choices directly shape the value a seller captures. The lesson for $50M+ operators is clear: buyers pay for predictability, not just performance.

Three things that move your multiple before you ever take a meeting:

1. Revenue quality matters more than revenue size. Recurring, contracted, and diversified income streams command higher multiples than lumpy project-based revenue, even at the same topline number.

2. Management depth is priced in. If the business cannot run without the founder for 90 days, buyers will discount accordingly. Build the bench now.

3. Clean financials reduce perceived risk. Audited statements and normalized EBITDA eliminate negotiating leverage buyers use to push your price down.

You are always either building toward a premium exit or drifting toward a discounted one. There is no neutral position.

What is the single biggest gap between where your business is today and what a buyer would actually pay for it?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank on business exit strategies made something very clear: owners who plan their exits early capture significantly more value than those who react to an offer.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this play out constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. The owners who maximize their multiple are not the ones with the best product. They are the ones who treated their exit as a strategic discipline, not a finish line.

That means understanding what buyers in your space actually value, knowing your EBITDA adjustments cold, and having a story that holds up under due diligence.

If you are scaling and have not stress-tested your business through a buyer's lens, now is the time to start.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U?oc=5

Exit planning is not a transaction. It is a discipline that starts long before any letter of intent lands on your desk.

That is the foundation of Chapter 2 in our forthcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond. The chapter, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two advisors who have sat across the table in real deals.

One thing they make clear: most owners leave money on the table not because of bad negotiating, but because of decisions made years earlier that quietly eroded their valuation. The good news is those decisions are reversible, if you act with enough runway.

There is a framework in this chapter that changes how you see every operational decision you make from this point forward.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does by default. A strategy is what your team does by design. And right now, the gap between those two things is costing you more than you think.

Gartner recently found that AI is saving sales teams significant time, but that time savings isn't converting into revenue growth unless sales leadership actively redirects it toward high-value activities. The tool isn't the strategy. The tool serves the strategy, if one exists.

Here's what scaling companies need to hear:

1. Time recovered without direction becomes distraction, not production.
2. Your top performers already have an informal strategy. Your job is to make it the company's strategy.
3. Revenue targets are not a sales strategy. They're a wish.

If your sales leader can't articulate your strategy in two sentences, you don't have one.

What would change in your organization if your entire sales team operated with the same intentionality as your best rep?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey on the economics of B2B growth makes something very clear: the threshold a company needs to hit just to survive, let alone thrive, has shifted significantly upward. Companies that were considered stable at modest growth rates are now exposed.

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this matters immediately. You cannot grow your way out of a strategy gap. More pipeline on top of a broken or absent sales strategy just accelerates the chaos.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Revenue climbs, but margins compress, the wrong customers come in, and the sales team operates on instinct rather than design.

Read the McKinsey piece and ask yourself honestly: does your current sales approach match the competitive environment it is actually operating in?

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have never stopped to measure that feeling.

Adweek recently explored how legacy brands become cultural icons, and the pattern is consistent: the companies that win long-term are obsessive about the emotional signal they send, not just the visual identity they maintain.

Here is what scaling companies miss:

1. Brand coherence breaks down fast between $50M and $200M. New hires, new channels, new markets, all diluting the original signal without anyone noticing until the damage is done.

2. Most mid-market companies confuse marketing activity with brand building. Running campaigns is not the same as owning a position in your customer's mind.

3. The companies that scale cleanly treat brand standards as an operational discipline, not a creative exercise. It lives in onboarding, sales scripts, and client communications, not just the style guide.

So here is the real question: If a prospect walked away from their first interaction with your company, what would they say it felt like?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive profiles Ulta's CMO and how the brand balances long-term brand building with the demands of omnichannel marketing. It is a masterclass in holding two things at once without letting either one collapse.

For companies scaling past $50M, this tension is real and it shows up fast. You need revenue now, so performance marketing takes over. Then six months later, nobody can articulate what your brand actually stands for.

The companies that scale well build brand and demand together, not in sequence. They treat brand consistency as infrastructure, not decoration.

If your marketing team is optimizing for clicks but not for what your company actually means to customers, that gap will cost you more than any ad budget.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

What does your marketing smell like? That is not a trick question. It is the opening challenge in Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

Chapter 5, written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, digs into something most scaling companies avoid: the gap between what leadership thinks the brand communicates and what customers actually experience.

When Adweek profiles leaders turning legacy brands into cultural icons, the common thread is intentionality. Nothing about how those brands show up is accidental. Kayli and Yasmin lay out a framework for bringing that same intentionality to companies in the $50M to $500M range, where brand discipline is most likely to slip and most expensive to ignore.

One insight teased early: your brand has a sensory signature whether you designed it or not. The question is whether you are controlling it.

Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost center waiting to become a crisis.

Most companies scaling past $50M default to headcount as the answer to every operational problem. More salespeople. More managers. More layers. The result is a bloated org that moves slower than it did at half the size.

SHRM's latest research on hiring trends makes something clear: the companies winning in 2026 are not hiring at volume. They are hiring with precision. Right role, right moment, right person for where the business is going, not where it has been.

Here is what that means in practice for leaders at your stage:

1. Your job architecture needs to lead your headcount decisions, not follow them.
2. The cost of a wrong hire at the director level and above is not just salary. It is 12 to 18 months of lost momentum.
3. Talent planning belongs in your quarterly business review, not just your annual budget cycle.

What would change in your organization if you treated every open role as a strategic decision rather than an operational one?

#TalentStrategy #ScalingBusiness #ExecutiveLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece in PCT magazine highlighted WorkWave's decision to bring on a new Chief Human Resources Officer as part of a broader leadership build-out.

On the surface, it reads like a routine executive announcement. But for companies in the $50M to $500M range, there is a real lesson underneath it.

The moment you need an HR leader is almost always six months before you realize it. Companies at scale do not struggle because the work is hard. They struggle because the people infrastructure never kept pace with the revenue growth.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. Founders and CEOs who nailed the first phase of growth suddenly find their talent systems are built for a $30M company trying to run a $100M one.

If your people strategy is still informal, reactive, or owned by no one specific, that is worth addressing now, not after the next growth push.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make your business smarter. They make it slower.

Most companies scaling past $50M make the same mistake: they treat metrics like a collection hobby. Every department adds its own dashboard. Every leader defends their numbers. And somewhere in a Tuesday morning meeting, nobody can agree on what is actually true.

Business.com recently catalogued 14 different tools companies use to track KPIs. Fourteen. The problem is not the tools. The problem is that most organizations have not decided what they are trying to measure before they start measuring it.

Here is what high-performance companies do differently:

1. They limit company-wide KPIs to five or fewer that directly tie to strategic priorities.
2. They assign one owner per metric, not a committee.
3. They review KPIs on a cadence that matches the speed of the decision they need to make, not just weekly because it feels disciplined.

If your leadership team cannot recite your top three KPIs without looking at a screen, you do not have a measurement problem. You have a clarity problem.

How many KPIs does your leadership team actually act on versus just report?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite breaks down 11 key KPIs for hospitality businesses, covering everything from occupancy rates to revenue per available room.

The list is solid. But here is what the article does not address: knowing which KPIs to track is only half the job. The harder work is deciding which ones your leadership team will actually make decisions from.

For companies scaling through $50M and beyond, KPI bloat is a real growth killer. When every department presents its own metrics with no connection to company-wide priorities, you end up with a lot of data and very little direction.

The question is not what can you measure. It is what will you act on.

Read the full article and think about which of your current KPIs would survive a hard cut: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMilAFBVV95cUxOU1pVUnJhVjRuTWxTYTJPdEhtNE5maTd5VHF3UWVJSXdwVW1jRFFJMXdKMkg3dWEzdmdzdHpaUnA0dWNIRGhYOTUyOGtDaW45LTU1UmllcXNwSVNYM0lUZU9qYi0xWmlMZTZVSWhPUVNaREV5N1RIaDlMSXpzNWI5RXdvbmVNLTdXX2pKcHZtQnpRQzZs

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every scaling company needs to read before their next planning cycle.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled "Death by KPIs." It was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, and it tackles something most leadership teams are too busy to confront: the moment your metrics stop driving performance and start creating noise.

One of the core ideas in the chapter is that the companies most at risk are not the ones ignoring data. They are the ones drowning in it. There is a point where adding another KPI actually reduces accountability rather than increasing it.

If your team spends more time building reports than acting on them, this chapter was written for you.

post1.text:
AI will not save your business. Your strategy around AI will.

Every week, another headline confirms that AI is lifting productivity across industries. Bloomberg recently surveyed twelve CEOs on how they use AI to reclaim hours in their week. The tools vary. The discipline behind them does not.

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M need to understand:

1. AI amplifies your existing systems. If your operations are loose, AI makes the looseness faster and cheaper to ignore until it becomes catastrophic.

2. The productivity gains are real, but they are not automatic. Companies capturing them have assigned ownership over AI adoption, not just access.

3. The executives winning with AI are not using more tools. They are using fewer tools with sharper intent tied to specific business outcomes.

The question for your leadership team is not whether to adopt AI. It is whether your organization has the structural discipline to absorb what AI surfaces.

What would your business reveal if AI suddenly made every inefficiency visible?

post2.text:
A recent piece in The New York Times explored a growing trend among busy executives: deploying AI twins to handle communications, meetings, and decisions on their behalf.

Fascinating concept. But for companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this raises a more urgent question than novelty.

At that growth stage, the bottleneck is rarely the CEO's calendar. It is the absence of systems that allow the organization to function without constant executive intervention. An AI twin built on top of a dependency-heavy culture is just a more expensive version of the same problem.

Autobahn works with leaders who want to scale the business, not just their own bandwidth. AI is a lever worth pulling, but only after the underlying structure is sound.

Read the full piece and think about what it means for how your organization is actually built: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifkFVX3lxTE1fZnBYemx0U1pIYUJQSk1WSm1sdThzLWNxcnJmaUNqMDFSajVISUtSXzJBTWFtSW9PY0JjcUVZSjRSaTZwblhuYWg3NUM1Xy1MVmxpSWtHSUJzRmlGZjA1VHBHczEwbkl5UmswVW1qVi00Q0Z3NUtZeHZDb0lEQQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Newsweek recently asked a sharp question: AI is boosting productivity, but is it actually worth it?

Chapter 8 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business tackles exactly this tension. Titled The Third Monitor Theory, the chapter was co-authored by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, and it reframes how growth-stage companies should think about AI adoption.

The insight that will stay with you: having access to AI and building a business capable of leveraging AI are two completely different problems. Most leadership teams are solving the first one while ignoring the second.

If your company is between $50M and $500M, that distinction is worth a serious conversation before your next technology investment.

The most dangerous leaders are the ones who never doubt themselves. Not the ones who do.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a flaw to fix. It is not. At the $50M+ level, the leaders who feel it most are often the ones carrying the most responsibility, making the highest-stakes calls, and thinking clearly enough to know what they do not know.

Forbes recently reported that imposter syndrome tends to intensify as leaders climb higher, not fade. That finding should reframe how scaling companies think about leadership development.

Here is what actually matters at this stage:

1. Self-doubt is not a signal to slow down. It is a signal to build better decision-making systems around you.

2. Leaders who acknowledge uncertainty earn more trust from their teams than those who project false confidence.

3. The goal is not to eliminate the feeling. It is to stop letting it delay action.

If your best leaders are quietly questioning whether they belong in the room, what does your culture do with that?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Seattle University outlines six practical ways leaders can work through imposter syndrome when stepping into a new role. It is worth a read, and it points to something we see constantly with companies scaling past $50M.

The leadership gaps that stall growth are rarely technical. They are psychological. Your operators, new executives, and even your founder can be making sound decisions while privately convinced they are one bad quarter away from being exposed.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who have built real businesses and still carry this weight. Naming it and building structures around it is not soft work. It is how you protect the company from leadership paralysis at the worst possible moments.

post1.text:
Work-life balance is the wrong goal. At the $50M to $500M growth stage, chasing balance will stall your company and exhaust you faster.

What high-performing leaders at that level actually need is intentional life design. Not balance. Design.

Recent reporting on Latina entrepreneurs building meaningful businesses from the ground up reinforces a pattern we see constantly: the founders who scale without burning out are not the ones who work less. They are the ones who decide in advance what their life is supposed to look like and build the business around that vision.

Three things scaling leaders get wrong about this:

1. They treat personal planning as a reward for business success rather than a prerequisite for it.
2. They assume their team cannot handle more responsibility, so they never create space for themselves.
3. They confuse being busy with being strategic.

Your business has a growth plan. Does your life?

#BusinessLeadership #ScalingUp #LifeDesign

post2.text:
A recent piece in TODAY.com featured five Latina entrepreneurs sharing hard-won advice about building businesses on their own terms. What stood out was not the hustle. It was how deliberately each of them protected their identity, values, and personal vision while scaling.

For companies moving through the $50M to $500M range, that intentionality is not a soft skill. It is a competitive advantage.

Leaders who have not defined what they are building toward personally tend to make reactive decisions professionally. They over-hire, under-delegate, and burn through leadership capacity at exactly the wrong moment.

The companies we see scale cleanly are led by people who have done the inner work alongside the strategic work.

Worth a read if you are building something significant and want to stay intact while doing it.
